A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same CoCoEmo study. Their main text, equations, figures, tables, and Appendices A–I are readable and support reliable matching of retained and added material.

before.justification: v1 reports original cross-conditioning, representation-probing, and speech-synthesis experiments, including objective measurements and human naturalness ratings.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and additionally reports baseline-scaling, EmoSteer-TTS comparison, and joint-module steering results.

M1.justification: The proposed method retains the same layer selection, mean-difference vectors, weighted emotion composition, additive activation steering, and renormalization. Joint SLM/flow steering is evaluated as an experimental alternative in Appendix F.2, without changing the proposed SLM-only procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use ESD, RAVDESS, CREMA-D, and IEMOCAP with the same English single-emotion, mixed-emotion, and text–emotion mismatch coverage. The added experiments reuse existing mixed-emotion evaluation scenarios on CREMA-D and IEMOCAP.

E2.justification: EmoSteer-TTS, merely cited in v1, becomes an evaluated comparator on CosyVoice2 in v2 Table 8. Table 9 also compares a joint SLM/flow-steering alternative against CoCoEmo. Existing native-control and diagnostic comparators are retained.

E3.justification: New experiments sweep IndexTTS2 emotion-vector scaling from 0.1 to 0.8, EmoSteer strength from 0.5 to 2.0, and a shared joint-module strength from 0.5 to 2.5. Existing splits, metrics, and main settings remain unchanged; the default 0.6 emotion-vector scaling was already documented in v1 Appendix E.1.

E4.justification: Appendix E.3 adds a systematic baseline-scaling sensitivity analysis, while Appendix F.2 directly tests whether adding flow steering benefits the central SLM-only design. These substantially extend the component and sensitivity evidence, documenting speaker-preservation tradeoffs and degradation under strong joint steering.

E5.justification: The MOS averaging, 10–13 listener description, and CCC mean/standard-deviation description are retained. v2 adds no repeated-run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests; the new comparisons report point estimates.

E6.justification: Existing numerical tables remain unchanged, including v1 Tables 7–9, now Tables 10–12. New Tables 7–9 substantially expand results on scaling and module tradeoffs. For example, IEMOCAP joint steering at alpha 1.5 yields correlation 0.246 and speaker similarity 0.869, versus 0.215 and 0.890 for SLM-only steering at alpha 5.0; joint alpha 2.5 yields WER 20.93.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and equations for extraction, composition, inference, rater consensus, and CCC are retained. A mixing-weight notation correction and additional linear-representation citations introduce no substantive mathematical revision, derivation, or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract and principal introduction/conclusion claims retain their scope: locating emotional control in the SLM, enabling compositional and text-independent steering, and evaluating mixed emotions through multi-rater annotations. Additional experiments support these existing contributions.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive limitations concerning temporal control, discrete-label extraction, free-form control interfaces, missing subjective emotion-faithfulness evaluation, and unexplored nonlinear geometry. Section 4.2 acknowledges OOD naturalness losses, and Appendix F.2 interprets joint steering as interference, although its results also show some emotion-control gains.

D1.justification: v2 replaces v1's promise of future code release with a concrete repository address; repository contents cannot be verified from the PDFs. It also documents shared extraction data and the tied-strength procedure for the added comparisons. Existing architecture, hook, and baseline implementation details remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds Park et al. (2024) and Reichman et al. (2025) to connect steering with linear representations and emotional directions in text LLMs. It also explicitly positions CoCoEmo against the previously cited EmoSteer-TTS flow-steering approach. The broader related-work discussion is retained.

P1.justification: Edits include renaming Section 2 from 'Disentangling' to 'Analyzing,' localized grammar corrections, updated affiliation/publication text and acknowledgements, and new limitations and appendix subsections. Most prose and the overall narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: Figure 1 is redrawn and enlarged, especially its vector-construction panels. v2 adds three appendix tables, groups Figures 10–12 together, and relocates or resizes some retained displays. Existing result tables and plots otherwise retain their structure and content.

improvement.justification: The direct EmoSteer-TTS comparison, joint-module ablation, and scaling sweep make the design choices and control–quality tradeoffs more assessable than in v1. Explicit limitations and code-access information also improve transparency. The gain is limited by overgeneralized interpretations: Table 8 includes tied or slightly better emotion-control results for EmoSteer-TTS, and Table 9 shows an IEMOCAP control gain from joint steering despite quality costs. These additions strengthen the evidence without fully supporting blanket superiority claims.
